DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
# Review: Menu Pricing Review, Spring 2026

The price increases may well be sensible, but the paper is less well evidenced than its author believes. It has one factual error that reverses a recommendation, it leaves the beef cost rise out of the projection, and it may compute margins on VAT-inclusive prices. I've checked every figure; the arithmetic in Table 1 and in section 5.3 is correct.

## Major issues

### 1. The risotto has the *best* margin on the menu, not the weakest

Recalculating Table 1 confirms the paper's own margins:

| Dish | Price | Cost | Margin | GP per plate | Weekly GP |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | £11.40 | £3,534 |
| Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | £10.80 | £2,808 |
| Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | £10.90 | £1,962 |
| Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | £15.60 | £1,872 |
| **Mushroom risotto** | £14.00 | £2.80 | **80%** | **£11.20** | £1,008 |

At 80%, the risotto has the highest margin of any dish. Its cash profit per plate is higher than the curry's and the burger's. Its 90 plates a week also tie with the specials rather than being uniquely lowest. The rationale in section 5.2 is therefore wrong on both counts.

Replacing the risotto probably *reduces* profit. If the seasonal special performs like the existing specials (64% margin) at the same £14 price, gross profit per plate falls from £11.20 to about £8.96. That loses about **£200 a week** (around £10,500 a year) at current volumes. The risotto may also be the only permanent vegetarian main. Removing it risks losing whole tables, not just 90 plates.

**Recommendation:** Drop proposal 5.2. Alternatively, reframe it as a test, with a cost target for the special of at least 80% margin.

### 2. The projection ignores the 12% beef price rise

Section 4 reports a 12% rise in beef prices from 1 April, the same day as the new prices. But section 5.3 assumes costs are unchanged.

- **Steak:** £10.40 × 12% ≈ £1.25 more per plate. That eats over 60% of the £2 increase, so the net gain is about £0.75 rather than £2.00.
- **Burger:** If the whole £4.20 cost were beef, it would rise by up to £0.50, halving the £1 increase. In reality the bun, garnish and fries are not beef, so the true figure is somewhat lower.

Together these reduce the gain by up to about **£280 a week**. That takes the £810 down to about **£530 a week, or roughly £27,500 a year**. It also undermines the 71% margin claim. On my estimate the margin moves to about 69%, not 71%, so the 70% target is still not met. (This estimate assumes the specials sell at roughly £16; their price isn't given.)

### 3. Margins may be calculated on VAT-inclusive prices

UK menu prices include 20% VAT, and Table 1's margins are computed on those prices. On ex-VAT revenue, the margins are noticeably lower:

| Dish | Margin on menu price | Margin ex-VAT |
|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | 69% | 63% |
| Steak | 60% | 52% |

Likewise, a £1 menu increase yields only about £0.83 of revenue. The £810 a week becomes about **£675 before the beef cost adjustment**, and around **£400 a week (≈£20,500 a year) after it**.

If the 70% target was set on a VAT-inclusive basis, then the comparison is at least consistent. Either way, the paper should state the basis it uses. The owners will judge the profit against accounts that exclude VAT.

## Moderate issues

### 4. "Volumes will hold" is asserted, not tested

The paper gives no sensitivity analysis. Here are the break-even points, ignoring VAT and beef costs:

| Dish | Volume can fall by | Before the increase loses money |
|---|---|---|
| Fish and chips | ~8% | ~25 plates/week |
| Burger | ~8.5% | ~22 plates/week |
| Steak | ~11% | ~14 plates/week |

These are small margins. Some of the supporting evidence is weak:

- **Repeat guests:** 60% repeat bookings shows loyalty, not price insensitivity. Regulars are the guests most likely to notice increases.
- **The 2024 price change:** "No visible effect on bookings" is anecdotal. It also measures bookings, not plates, covers or walk-ins.
- **Weekday lunch:** This trade is called price-sensitive and "a small share," but it isn't quantified.

### 5. The monitoring plan can't detect a problem reliably

Comparing April and May volumes with a January–February baseline mixes the effect of the price change with the seasonal effect. Spring trade, including Easter, normally rises above the winter low. Volumes could therefore look stable or higher even if the price rises are costing sales. Use the same weeks of 2025 as the baseline, adjusted for the overall trend.

The plan also has no trigger for action. The break-even figures above give natural thresholds. For example, review fish and chips if volumes fall more than 5% against the seasonal baseline.

### 6. "Remain the value option" is no longer true

The midpoint claim checks out: £17.50 < £17.98, £16.00 < £16.50, and £28.00 < £29.50. But all three new prices are above the *lowest* competitor price for each dish (£16.95, £15.50 and £27.00). The Copper Kettle would no longer be the cheapest in the group, which is currently its position. Competitors facing the same beef increase may also raise their prices, which would help. Either way, the paper should say so rather than imply it is still the cheapest.

## Minor issues

7. **Trading days:** The recommendation says "six trading days a week," but section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday, which is five. This doesn't affect the annual figure, since that is weekly × 52, but it should be corrected.
8. **"Lowest in the group":** Section 3 says this of current prices, but no comparison is given for the curry or the risotto.
9. **Baseline season:** The data come from January–February, the quietest season, so they may misstate the usual mix of dishes.
10. **Silent increases:** Not drawing attention to the rises is a reasonable choice. But staff should be ready for regulars who ask.

## The author's description against the document

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| "Every main course" in the till data | Specials appear only as a single aggregated line. |
| "Full competitor price check" | Only three of the five main dishes were checked. |
| "Latest supplier information" | It was gathered, but not applied to the projection. |
| £810 a week, "simple to check" | The arithmetic is correct, but the gain is overstated, by about a third once beef costs are included and by half if VAT applies. |
| Margin lifted to "about 71%" | Only if costs stay flat, which section 4 says they won't. |
| Risotto has "the weakest margin" | **Incorrect.** It has the strongest. |
| "Low-risk and well evidenced" | The price rises are probably low-risk. The risotto proposal isn't, and the evidence on volumes is thin. |

## Suggested revisions

1. Withdraw or rework the risotto proposal.
2. Recompute the projection with the beef costs, stating whether VAT is included, and present a range rather than a single figure.
3. Add break-even volumes for each dish and use them as monitoring triggers.
4. Compare volumes with the same period in 2025 instead of January–February.
5. Consider whether the burger and steak need slightly larger increases to offset the beef cost. The steak could rise to £28.50 and still sit below the competitor midpoint.
6. Correct "six trading days."

With these changes, the paper would support approving the three price increases. As it stands, it would lead the owners to remove their most profitable dish.
